paragraphs: Micro-aeration unlocks endogenous nitrogen removal in anaerobic digesters via metabolically versatile fermentative bacteria
Linpei Han, Lei Li *, Wenjie Ye, Jiaqi Huang, Yongli Liu, Chaoran Duan, Bin Zhan, Shangbang Guo, Xuya Peng
Key laboratory of the Three Gorges Reservoir Region's Eco-environments, Ministry of Education, Institute of Environment and Ecology, Chongqing University, Chongqing 400045, PR China

The synthetic wastewater was composed of the following components: chemical oxygen demand (COD) of 2030.34 mg/L, supplied as glucose; 15N-labeled ammonium nitrogen (15NH4+-N) at a concentration of 267.75 mg/L, provided as 15NH4Cl; calcium ions (Ca2+) at 10 mg/L, sourced from CaCl2; and magnesium ions (Mg2+) at 10 mg/L, derived from MgCl2. Additionally, a trace-element solution was incorporated at a concentration of 0.5 mL/L, containing the following per liter: 1.5 g of FeCl3·6H2O, 0.03 g of CuSO4·5H2O, 0.18 g of KI, 0.12 g of MnCl2·H2O, 0.06 g of Na2MoO4·2H2O, 0.12 g of ZnSO4·7H2O, 0.15 g of CoCl2·6H2O, and 10 g of EDTA. All chemicals used were of analytical grade and procured from reputable suppliers including Macklin, Sinopharm, or Aladdin (China). All solutions were prepared using Milli-Q water, which has a resistivity of 18.2 MΩ·cm.

Nitrogen isotopic compositions were determined in three phases: solid (sludge organic nitrogen), liquid (15NH4+, 15NO2-, and 15NO3-), and gas (N2 and N2O) during the stable-isotope tracing experiment. For the solid-phase organic nitrogen, washed, dried, and ground sludge samples were analyzed using an elemental analyzer coupled with an isotope-ratio mass spectrometer (Sercon Integra2 EA-IRMS) (Ouyang et al., 2021). In the liquid phase, all inorganic nitrogen species were converted to N2O prior to measurement: 15NH4+ was converted via hypobromite oxidation followed by an azide reaction; 15NO2- was converted through an azide reaction; and 15NO3- was reduced using the denitrifier method (Kim et al., 2023). The resulting N2O was pre-concentrated and introduced via a GasBench II interface to an isotope-ratio mass spectrometer (Thermo MAT 253) for measurement. In the headspace, N2O was pre-concentrated (Sercon Cryoprep) and measured with an isotope-ratio mass spectrometer (Sercon 20-22) (Wankel et al., 2017); N2 was pre-concentrated and analyzed using a GasBench system coupled with an isotope-ratio mass spectrometer (Thermo Delta V Advantage) (Ouyang et al., 2021). Samples from all phases (including the initial feed) were collected on days 0, 5, 10, and 20, and analyzed in triplicate.
1.3 Verification of micro-aerobic nitrogen removal under high-ammonia conditions

A 50-day batch experiment was conducted to evaluate the feasibility of the micro-aeration process for treating actual high-ammonia digestate. Pre-filtered (2-mm sieve) fresh digestate (initial COD 4193.70 mg/L, TAN 3167.44 mg/L) was utilized as the substrate without the addition of external sludge inoculation. Experiments were conducted in 1000 mL sealed serum bottles with a working volume of 800 mL at a temperature of 37 °C; the initial pH was maintained at 7.8 ± 0.1. Intermittent micro-aeration was implemented to sustain the peak oxidation-reduction potential (ORP) pulse at approximately -50 mV. A test group and a non-aerated control group were established. Samples were collected every 5 days, filtered using 0.45-μm hydrophilic PTFE syringe filters, and analyzed for TAN and COD to monitor nitrogen removal and substrate consumption. Each experimental condition was replicated in triplicate.
1.4 Routine physicochemical analyses and EPS fractionation

The oxidation–reduction potential (ORP) in each reactor was continuously monitored using an industrial-grade ORP electrode positioned 2 cm below the liquid surface, with data recorded at 10-s intervals using a digital data logger. Immediately after completion of Phase III of the isotope-tracing experiment, in situ spatial ORP profiling was performed to characterize the spatial distribution of the redox environment within the reactor.

Hydrogen and methane contents in the reactor headspace were determined by gas chromatography (Agilent 7890, Agilent Technologies, USA) equipped with a thermal conductivity detector. Gas-phase samples were collected at the end of each experimental phase.

Liquid samples were collected every three days during Phases I and II and daily during Phases III and IV. The samples were filtered through 0.45-μm membrane filters and analyzed for COD, TAN, nitrite nitrogen (NO2--N), nitrate nitrogen (NO3--N), total nitrogen (TN), and hydroxylamine (NH2OH). COD was determined using the dichromate method; TAN was measured by Nessler's reagent spectrophotometry; NO2--N was quantified using N-(1-naphthyl)-ethylenediamine spectrophotometry; NO3--N was determined by UV spectrophotometry; and TN was measured by alkaline persulfate digestion followed by UV spectrophotometry. Hydroxylamine concentration was determined using the 8-hydroxyquinoline method (Su et al., 2024). All spectrophotometric measurements were performed using a UV-Vis spectrophotometer (Agilent Cary 4000).

Sludge samples collected at the end of Phases II, III, and IV were used for extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) extraction. EPS was sequentially fractionated into soluble EPS (S-EPS), loosely bound EPS (LB-EPS), and tightly bound EPS (TB-EPS) according to Ye et al. (2025). Briefly, mixed sludge samples were centrifuged, and the resulting supernatant was collected as S-EPS. The remaining pellet was resuspended in preheated NaCl solution, vortexed, and centrifuged to obtain LB-EPS. The residual pellet was subsequently incubated in a 60 °C water bath and centrifuged to obtain TB-EPS. All EPS extracts were filtered through 0.45-μm membrane filters prior to analysis.

Sludge samples from the CK and MG groups were collected at the end of Phases II and IV. Total genomic DNA was extracted using the FastDNA Spin Kit for Soil (MP Biomedicals, USA). Metagenomic libraries were prepared according to the methodology described by Zhang et al. and sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform (PE150) (Zhang et al., 2022).

Raw paired-end reads underwent quality control and trimming utilizing fastp (v0.23.0). De novo assembly of the filtered reads was executed using MEGAHIT (v1.1.2). Contigs were binned into metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) employing MetaBAT2 (v2.12.1) with default parameters. The quality of the MAGs was evaluated using CheckM2 (v2.0.1), retaining only high-quality MAGs with completeness >90% and contamination <5% for subsequent analysis.

Redundant MAGs were dereplicated with dRep (v3.4.2) using a 99% average nucleotide identity (ANI) threshold, resulting in a non-redundant MAG set. Taxonomic classification of the non-redundant MAGs was conducted with GTDB-Tk (v2.4.1) against the Genome Taxonomy Database (GTDB).

Open reading frames (ORFs) were predicted using Prodigal (v2.6.3), and ribosomal RNA genes were identified with Barrnap (v0.8). To quantify the relative abundance of each MAG, quality-filtered reads from each sample were mapped back to the non-redundant MAG set using Bowtie2. Abundance was calculated as reads per kilobase per million mapped reads (RPKM) and subsequently normalized to the total RPKM values of all MAGs within the same sample to derive the relative abundance. Finally, functional annotation was performed by comparing the predicted gene sequences against the KEGG database using KOBAS 2.0 with an e-value cutoff of 1×10-5.

The sludge samples utilized for metaproteomic analysis were identical to those described for metagenomics in Section 1.5, specifically the CK and MG samples collected at the end of Phases II and IV. Total proteins were extracted using a phenol-ammonium acetate/methanol precipitation protocol. The protein concentration was determined via the bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay, while integrity was assessed through SDS-PAGE. Equal quantities of protein were reduced, alkylated, precipitated with acetone, and subsequently digested with trypsin at 37 °C overnight. The resulting peptides were desalted using HLB solid-phase extraction cartridges and lyophilized. Peptides were separated online utilizing an EASY-nLC 1200 nanoflow LC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and analyzed on a Q Exactive HF-X mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific), operated in data-dependent acquisition (DDA) mode, with peptide fragmentation achieved through higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD). Raw mass spectrometry data were processed for protein identification using Proteome Discoverer software. The search database was constructed by translating the coding sequences predicted from the matched metagenomic assemblies (as detailed in Section 1.5) into amino acid sequences, thereby enabling sample-specific protein identification and supporting subsequent functional assignment and host MAG tracing.

Three-dimensional transient computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations were conducted to quantify the oxygen mass transfer and mixing characteristics within the reactor under micro-aeration conditions. The simulation utilized a 1:1 geometric model of the actual experimental setup (serum bottle), where the main reactor had a diameter of 85 mm and a height of 100 mm. A cylindrical fine-pore diffuser, measuring 20 mm in both diameter and height, was positioned at the bottom to serve as the gas distributor.

The computational domain was discretized using an unstructured tetrahedral mesh. The Eulerian-Eulerian multiphase model was employed to describe the two-phase flow of gas (oxygen) and liquid (digestate). The liquid phase (digestate) was characterized as a Newtonian fluid with a density of 998.5 kg m-3 and a dynamic viscosity of 82 cP. The gas phase entered through the bottom face of the diffuser as a mass-flow inlet, set at 4 × 10-6 kg s-1. Turbulence was modeled using the standard κ-ε model, while the top of the reactor was configured as an outlet to facilitate gas escape. The governing equations were solved transiently using a finite-volume-based solver. Pressure-velocity coupling was managed by the phase-coupled SIMPLE algorithm, and convective terms were discretized employing the second-order upwind scheme.

To quantitatively assess the mixing efficiency of the aeration system, a velocity uniformity index (UI) was calculated. The UI is defined as the volume-weighted average of the absolute difference between the velocity in each mesh cell and the volume-averaged velocity in the reactor. To quantitatively track the transformation and fate of nitrogen under micro-aeration, a 15N mass-balance calculation was performed based on the measured concentrations and 15N atom-percent contents of individual nitrogen pools. This calculation aimed to convert concentration data into the absolute mass of 15N in each phase. The mass of 15N in the liquid-phase inorganic nitrogen pools (NH4+-N, NO3--N, and NO2--N) was obtained by multiplying the concentration of each nitrogen species by the effective reactor volume on the corresponding sampling day and its 15N atom-percent content. The effective reactor volume decreased slightly due to sampling, measuring 0.40, 0.39, 0.38, and 0.37 L on days 0, 5, 10, and 20, respectively. For the solid phase, the mass of 15N in the sludge organic nitrogen was calculated by multiplying the sludge concentration (determined according to the Chinese industry standard CJ/T 221-2023), the mass fraction of organic nitrogen in the sludge, the effective reactor volume (as previously mentioned), and the 15N atom-percent content of the organic nitrogen. The mass of 15N in the gaseous nitrogen pools (N2 and N2O) was calculated by multiplying the molar concentration of the gas, the headspace gas volume, the number of nitrogen atoms per molecule (2 for both N2 and N2O), the molar mass of 15N (15 g·mol-1), and the gas's 15N atom-percent content.

Supplementary Figure 1. Performance of the micro-aeration process treating actual high-ammonia digestate. Temporal profiles of TAN and COD during the 50-day verification experiment. Data are mean ± s.d. from three independent replicates (n = 3).

Supplementary Figure 2. DFT analysis of intermolecular interactions between tryptophan molecules. Tryptophan was selected as a model aromatic amino acid residue to evaluate potential intermolecular interactions relevant to extracellular proteins. Among the modeled configurations, the carboxyl–carboxyl association exhibited the most favorable interaction energy (−26.09 kcal mol-1), indicating favorable intermolecular association under the modeled conditions. The corresponding frontier-orbital energy gap was 3.40 eV, providing additional information on the electronic characteristics of this configuration. These results demonstrate the potential of tryptophan molecules to form energetically favorable intermolecular associations and provide molecular-level support for possible protein-mediated interactions within EPS matrices. Atom colors are as follows: gray, carbon; red, oxygen; white, hydrogen; and blue, nitrogen.

Supplementary Figure 3. Quality-control metrics of the metaproteomic dataset. (a) Mass-error distribution of identified peptides. Deviations were centered near 0 ppm, with most peptides falling within ±10 ppm, confirming the high mass accuracy of the LC-MS/MS system. (b) Distribution of protein-sequence coverage. (c) Frequency distribution of unique peptides per protein group, following a typical power-law pattern. (d) Peptide-length distribution. The distribution was bell-shaped and peaked at 10–15 amino acids, consistent with the expected tryptic cleavage pattern. (e) Molecular-weight distribution of identified proteins. (f) Summary statistics of the identification workflow, listing the total numbers of precursor ions, identified spectra, peptides, and protein groups.

Supplementary Figure 4. Genomic repertoire of nitrogen-metabolism genes in candidate nitrogen-removing MAGs. Twenty-one MAGs were selected as candidate nitrogen-removing populations based on the presence of key nitrogen-cycle genes and the detection of their corresponding proteins. Each circle represents one MAG. Inner colored bubbles indicate the copy numbers of genes associated with nitrification, denitrification, or dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonia (DNRA), with bubble size proportional to copy number, ranging from 1 to 5. MAGs encoding hydroxylamine oxidoreductase (hao), a key marker for ammonia oxidation, are highlighted with a pale-yellow background.

Supplementary Figure 5. Differential expression profiles of functional proteins across operational phases. Volcano plots show comparative metaproteomic profiles between the MG and CK groups during (a) Phase II and (b) Phase IV. Horizontal dashed lines indicate the statistical-significance threshold, −lg(adjusted p value) = 1.3, corresponding to adjusted p < 0.05. Vertical dashed lines denote the fold-change threshold, |log2FC| = 0.585, corresponding to FC > 1.5 or FC < 0.67. Data points are color-coded according to the log2FC gradient, with red indicating upregulated proteins and blue indicating downregulated proteins. Point size is proportional to −lg(adjusted p value). Key nitrogen-metabolism enzymes are labeled. Repeated labels for the same enzyme, such as NirS and NosZ, represent distinct protein variants derived from different MAGs that collectively contribute to community-level functions. Proteins associated with the ammonia monooxygenase and particulate methane monooxygenase complexes were absent from the metaproteomic dataset.
Supplementary Figure 6. Community-level metagenomic evidence of nitrogen metabolism genes under micro-aeration.

Supplementary Figure 7. Multi-omics evidence supporting the potential hydrogen-utilizing autotrophic metabolism of MAG415. The upper panels show carbon-fixation and hydrogen-oxidation modules encoded and expressed in MAG415, including RuBisCO (RbcL/CbbL), Prk, and hydrogenases. Gray symbols indicate absent genes, blue triangles indicate genes detected in the genome, and blue squares indicate corresponding proteins detected in the metaproteome. Heatmaps show protein abundances (log2LFQ) in the CK and MG groups during Phase II. The lower panel illustrates a putative metabolic linkage between H2 utilization, respiratory electron transfer, and nitrogen transformation, in which H2-derived electrons may contribute reducing equivalents to downstream nitrogen transformation.

Supplementary Figure 8. Reconstructed downstream C1-oxidation potential and protein-abundance patterns in Methylocaldum sp. MAG600. The left panel shows a reconstructed C1-oxidation scheme from methane to CO₂. The initial methane-to-methanol oxidation step mediated by particulate methane monooxygenase (pMMO), encoded by pmoABC, was not annotated in MAG600 and is therefore shown as an unannotated module (red arrow). This absence contrasts with the genetic repertoire for downstream oxidation of methanol, formaldehyde, and formate (blue arrows). The right panel shows a heatmap of identified C1-metabolism enzyme abundances, expressed as log2LFQ, across operational phases. Sustained high expression of methanol dehydrogenases (Mdh1 and XoxF) and the formaldehyde-activating enzyme Fae indicates that MAG600 primarily functions as a methylotroph, scavenging methanol-derived intermediates in this niche rather than initiating methane oxidation.

Supplementary Figure 9. Protein-abundance patterns of selected carbon-salvage, central-metabolism, and micro-oxic respiration markers in MAG600. Bubble plots show the comparative abundances, expressed as log2LFQ, of selected proteins between the CK and MG groups at the end of Phase II. Bubble size corresponds to protein abundance, with pink and blue colors representing the CK and MG conditions, respectively.

Supplementary Figure 10. Differences in the abundance of key methanogenic genes between the MG and CK groups. The figure shows the impact of micro-aeration on the functional gene repertoire involved in methanogenesis. The background shows the core methanogenic pathways, with blue, gray, and yellow arrows denoting the acetoclastic, hydrogenotrophic, and methylotrophic routes, respectively, all converging at the terminal step indicated by a red arrow. Adjacent to each key enzyme or gene, a colored matrix shows its relative abundance, expressed as the percentage based on KEGG annotation, across four samples: CK and MG groups during Phase II and Phase IV. The color scale indicates abundance levels ranging from blue, 0%, to red, 0.030%.
